scenes.narration: What would you do if someone offered you a barrel of oil, and paid you to take it?

On April twentieth, twenty twenty, that is exactly what happened. The price of American crude oil for delivery in May fell below zero, for the first time since that contract began trading in nineteen eighty-three. At the end of the day it settled at minus thirty-seven dollars and sixty-three cents a barrel. People who owned oil were paying others to take it off their hands. To understand how, you have to understand that an oil price is really a promise, and on that day the promise came due.

scenes.narration: What happens to oil when the world stops moving?

In the spring of twenty twenty, the pandemic shut down much of the planet. Planes stayed on the ground. Roads emptied. Factories went quiet. Analysts cited by the US Congressional Research Service estimated that global demand for crude oil fell by about thirty million barrels a day, around thirty percent of everything the world normally burns.

The big producers tried to respond. On April twelfth, the OPEC Plus group agreed to cut output by nine point seven million barrels a day, the largest single production cut in history. But it would only start in May. And even a record cut was much smaller than the hole in demand.

Let me draw the problem. Here is the oil coming out of the ground every day. Here is the oil the world was actually using. The gap between them did not disappear. Every barrel nobody wanted had to go somewhere. Into a tank, a pipeline, or a ship. And the space in those tanks was running out.

scenes.narration: To see why that mattered so much, you need to know how oil is really traded.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: When you buy oil on the market, what do you actually own?

Most oil is traded through futures contracts. A futures contract is a promise to buy or sell barrels of oil at a set price, on a set date in the future. The best known American contract is called W T I. Each month has its own contract, and each one ends on a fixed day. The May twenty twenty contract expired on April twenty-first.

And here is the key. These contracts are for real oil. According to the US Energy Information Administration, anyone still holding one when it expires must make or take physical delivery of crude oil in Cushing, Oklahoma, a small town that is home to a major oil storage hub.

keyframes.cue: These contracts are for real oil
keyframes.label: items[0].stampAt.cue

scenes.narration: Let me draw what that means. Here is a trader who bought a May contract. Before the expiry date, they have two choices. Sell the contract to someone else. Or keep it, and receive real barrels of oil in Oklahoma, and find somewhere to put them. Most financial traders have no tanks and no pipelines. So for them, there is only one real choice. Sell before the deadline.

Most people did leave in time. According to the US regulator, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the number of open May contracts fell from about six hundred and thirty-five thousand at the start of April to about one hundred and nine thousand on the morning of April twentieth. But that still left a lot of contracts, with one day to go.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: And to take delivery, you need one thing above all. Somewhere to put the oil.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: What happens when the tanks are full?

The storage tanks at Cushing can hold about seventy-six million barrels of crude oil. In mid-March, they were about half full. By April seventeenth, they held sixty million barrels. They were seventy-six percent full, and filling fast. The three weeks to April seventeenth brought the three largest weekly increases ever recorded.

And seventy-six percent full did not mean twenty-four percent free. As the Energy Information Administration noted, some of the empty space had probably already been leased or promised to someone else. For a trader looking for a tank at the last minute, there was almost nothing left.

Oil companies started looking for storage anywhere they could find it, including at sea. In the first three weeks of April, the oil stored on tankers floating offshore rose by almost sixty-nine million barrels, to about one hundred and twenty-seven million barrels. Ships became floating warehouses.

And the tanks kept filling after the crash. A week later, on April twenty-fourth, Cushing was eighty-one percent full. By the start of May, according to the Energy Information Administration, it had reached eighty-three percent of its working capacity. The hub was never completely full. But for anyone holding a May contract with nowhere to send the oil, it did not need to be.

Let me draw what storage does to a price. Normally, a barrel today and a barrel next month cost about the same. But when storage runs out, oil for delivery right now becomes a burden. You have to pay someone to keep it. So the near month falls, and the later months hold up. The gap between them is the price of a tank.

scenes.narration: On Friday, April seventeenth, the May contract closed at eighteen dollars and twenty-seven cents. Then came Monday.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: How can the price of something real fall below nothing?

On Monday, April twentieth, the last full trading day before expiry, the May contract started falling and kept falling. Holders who could not take delivery needed to sell. But there were very few buyers with somewhere to put the oil. By the early afternoon in New York, the price was approaching zero.

Then it went through the floor. According to the regulator, in twenty minutes, between eight minutes past two and twenty-eight minutes past two, the price fell from zero to minus thirty-nine dollars and fifty-five cents. A minute later it hit minus forty dollars and thirty-two cents, the lowest price in the history of the contract.

scenes.narration: At the close, the May contract settled at minus thirty-seven dollars and sixty-three cents. From the start of trading to the bottom, it had lost fifty-eight dollars and five cents a barrel. Some sellers were, in effect, paying a counterparty to let them out of their contracts.

The strangest number was the gap between two months. On Friday, May oil had been about seven dollars cheaper than June oil. By Monday's close, the gap was fifty-eight dollars. The June contract, for the same oil delivered just one month later, closed at twenty dollars and forty-three cents. Nothing had happened to the oil itself. Only to the date.

Let me draw that Monday. Here is the May contract on Friday, eighteen dollars. Here is the June contract on Monday, still around twenty dollars. And here is the May contract at the close, almost thirty-eight dollars below zero. The same oil, the same pipeline, one month apart. All the other months stayed above zero. Only the one that was about to arrive collapsed.

scenes.narration: The next morning, the world woke up to headlines about negative oil. But the story was not over.

keyframes.cue: But the story was not over
keyframes.label: The story was not over

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Who was left holding the oil?

On April twenty-first, its last day, the May contract settled at ten dollars and one cent, positive again. But the panic spread to the next month. The June contract fell by forty-three percent that day, to eleven dollars and fifty-seven cents.

The regulator later looked at who was trading. On April twentieth, out of four hundred and forty-eight large traders it tracked, one hundred and seventy-three still held May contracts. Its interim report described the conditions in detail, but did not name a single cause for the crash.

The exchange had seen the risk coming. In early April, CME Group sent notices to its members about the possibility of negative prices, and opened a testing system so that trading firms could check that their computers could handle a price below zero. In almost forty years of trading, that had never happened before.
As lockdowns eased and demand slowly returned, the price recovered. By July first, a barrel of American oil was back at about forty dollars. Prices below zero had not even lasted two trading days.

So what does negative oil teach about prices? That a price is not just about how useful something is. It is also about where it is, when it arrives, and whether you have room for it. On April twentieth, the oil had not lost its value. The world had simply run out of places to put it. And a contract that looked like a piece of paper turned out to be a promise to take delivery of something very real.
